stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate test for short-term memory?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Working memory is synonymous is synonymous with short-term memory, which is responsible for the immediate recall of small amounts of verbal (as in digit span) or visuospatial information.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 82.

stem: Which type of memory is most relatively well preserved in schizophrenia?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Spatial working memory, short-term and long-term memory, working memory, episodic memory, and semantic memory have all been found to be impaired in people with schizophrenia, compared to health controls.
reference: Gebreegziabhere Y et al. Cognitive impairment in people with schizophrenia: an umbrella review. European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience. 2022 Oct;272(7):1139-55.

stem: What is the pathophysiologic mechanism of Wernicke-Korsako syndrome?
explanation:
EXPLANATION: Wernicke encephalopathy (WE) and Korsako psychosis, together termed Wernicke-Korsako syndrome, are distinct yet overlapping neuropsychiatric disorders associated with thiamine deficiency. Deficiency of thiamine can lead to decreased functioning of enzymes involved in the tricarboxylic acid cycle (alpha-keto glutamate dehydrogenase and pyruvate dehydrogenase), pentose phosphate pathway, and branched-chain amino acid metabolism. Mammillary body lesions are the classic autopsy sign in WE patients and are present in almost all cases. Location of mammillary bodies is shown in the attached figure adapted from Meys et al. American Journal of Neuroradiology. 2022 Jun 1;43(6):802-12.

encephalopathy and Korsako psychosis. Journal of basic and clinical physiology and pharmacology. 2018 Oct 2;30(2):153-62.

stem: It is understood that the consolidation of emotional memories occurs in which stage of sleep?
options: Consolidation of memories does not occur during sleep
explanation: EXPLANATION: Evidence for the role of REM sleep in consolidation of the emotional components of memory is relatively strong. The precise mechanisms by which REM sleep promotes consolidation of emotional memories remains unresolved, although there are some studies suggesting that long-term potentiation processes are activated in REM sleep. There is a large body of literature suggesting that theta oscillations, characteristic of REM sleep, play a role in memory consolidation, particularly in fear conditioning and emotional memories.
reference: Sara SJ. Sleep to remember. Journal of Neuroscience. 2017 Jan 18;37(3):457-63.

stem: What is the pathophysiologic mechanism of multisystem atrophy?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Multisystem atrophy (MSA), a family of Parkinson-plus diseases, includes a cerebellar type (formerly olivopontocerebellar degeneration) that is notable for ataxia and a subtype with pronounced autonomic dysfunction (formerly Shy-Drager syndrome). There is a common neuropathological finding of distinctive inclusion bodies in glial cells which contain alpha-synuclein, leading to the classification of MSA as a synucleinopathy. No mutations in the gene for alpha-synuclein have been found in MSA, which appears to exist only as a sporadic disorder.
reference: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9th Edition. 2023. p. 423. Gray F, Duyckaerts C, de Girolami U. Escourolle and Poirier’s Manual of Basic Neuropathology, 6th Edition. 2019. p. 204.

stem: Which of the following is an important component of the blood brain barrier (BBB)?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Cerebrovascular homeostasis is maintained by the blood-brain barrier (BBB), a highly selective structure that separates the peripheral blood circulation from the brain and protects the central nervous system. Several recent studies have highlighted the importance of the physiological role of the beta-amyloid precursor protein (APP) in endothelial cell homeostasis, suggesting an important role of this protein in maintaining vascular stability.
reference: Ristori E et al. New insights into blood-brain barrier maintenance: the homeostatic role of ß-amyloid precursor protein in cerebral vasculature. Frontiers in Physiology. 2020 Aug 27;11:1056.

stem: Brain organoids can mimic which age of the human brain?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Brain organoids are produced by the differentiation of pluripotent stem cells under three-dimensional culture conditions by adding neurodevelopment- related regulatory signals. They are similar to the cell composition and anatomical structure of the brain, and can reflect the developmental process of the bring, as well as their physiology, pathology, and pharmacology. In terms of their cellular and molecular composition, the current architecture of brain organoids can mimic the second-trimester human fetal brain.
reference: Chen H et al. Brain organoids: Establishment and application. Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology. 2022 Nov 23;10:1029873.

stem: Dysfunction in which neurotransmitter is likely to contribute the most to cognitive symptoms in schizophrenia?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Although dopamine dysfunction has mainly been linked to positive psychotic symptoms, striatal dopamine signalling normally has widespread effects on cortical function, and its dysregulation can also cause cognitive symptoms. Many researchers believe that cognitive and some negative symptoms of schizophrenia may be due to a deficit of dopamine activity in mesocortical projections to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
reference: McCutcheon RA et al. Cognitive impairment in schizophrenia: aetiology, pathophysiology, and treatment. Molecular psychiatry. 2023 Jan 23:1-7. Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscienti c Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 95.

stem: The processing of empathy is most influenced by which of the following structures?
explanation: EXPLANATION: The anterior insula cortex has been shown to be a core circuit for empathy.
reference: Li Y et al. Linking brain structure and activation in anterior insula cortex to explain the trait empathy for pain. Human brain mapping. 2020 Mar;41(4):1030-42.

stem: Which of the following is recommended for the treatment of REM sleep behaviour disorder?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Recommended treatments for REM sleep behaviour disorder include clonazepam, melatonin, and pramipexole. Melatonin binds to the M1 and M2 receptors, suppressing REM sleep motor tone and renormalising other circadian features of REM sleep. Melatonin requires a prescription in the EU and the UK.
reference: Howell M. Management of REM sleep behavior disorder: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline. Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine. 2023 Apr 1;19(4):759-68.

stem: Loss of orexin-producing neurons takes place in which condition?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Orexin/hypocretin neurons are localised exclusively in certain hypothalamic areas (later hypothalamic area, perifornical area, and posterior hypothalamus). These hypothalamic neurons degenerate in narcolepsy, and loss of these neurons causes the inability of orexin to be produced and released downstream on wake-promoting neurotransmitter centres and thus lack of stabilising wakefulness.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscienti c Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 407.

stem: In Bayesian theory, what is the term given to an expected result or belief?
explanation: EXPLANATION: The account of predictive processing has emerged as an alluring computational model to explain how brain processes information about the world. In the higher brain centers, expected predictions and pre-existing beliefs (known as priors) are said to be combined with observed sensory data (referred to as likelihood) to compute a posterior probability (referred to as the posterior). This posterior probability is said to represent the most probable perception, considering both the prior beliefs and the sensory evidence. In cases where there is a disparity between the prior expectations and the sensory evidence (likelihood), a prediction error is generated. This error signal initiates the necessity to revise the brain's current model and adjust its prior beliefs accordingly. To express it formally, a prediction error quantifies the difference between the means of the prior and likelihood distributions, taking into account their respective precisions (inverse variance).
reference: Wilson P, Humpston C, Nathan R. Innovations in the psychopathology of schizophrenia: a primer for busy clinicians. BJPsych Advances. 2022 Mar;28(2):79-89.

stem: Which of the following protein inclusion profiles is most common in FTD?
explanation: EXPLANATION: The classification of frontotemporal dementias is based on the type of protein inclusions observed in neurons as well as the mutational status, if known. The inclusions contain predominantly or exclusively one of three markers: tau; TDP-43, a DNA/RNA-binding protein; and FUS (fused in sarcoma). Atypical frontotemporal lobar degeneration with ubiquitin-positive inclusion is a relatively rare cause of FTD characterised by FUS-positive inclusions.
reference: Gray F, Duyckaerts C, de Girolami U. Escourolle and Poirier’s Manual of Basic Neuropathology, 6th Edition. 2019. p. 192. Peet BT et al. Neuroimaging in frontotemporal dementia: heterogeneity and relationships with underlying neuropathology. Neurotherapeutics. 2021 Apr;18:728-52.

stem: How many times does a G protein coupled receptor pass through the cell membrane?
explanation: EXPLANATION:Receptors linked to G proteins all have the structure of seven- transmembrane regions, meaning that they span the membrane seven times.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscienti c Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 36.

stem: Purines
options: Can only be obtained from the diet
explanation: EXPLANATION: A purine is an aromatic heterocycle composed of carbon and nitrogen. Eukaryotes, bacteria, and archaea are all able to carry out de-novo biosynthesis of purines. Purines include adenine and guanine, which participate in DNA and RNA formation. Purines are also constituents of other important biomolecules, such as ATP, GTP, cyclic AMP, NADH, and coenzyme A. Other important purines include hypoxanthine, xanthine, theobromine, caffeine, uric acid, and isoguanine. Cytosine, thymine, and uracil are pyrimidines.
reference: Kumari, A. Chapter 17 - Purine Structures in Sweet Biochemistry, 2018. pp. 89-91.

stem: Which of the following candidate genes form the most biologically plausible genetic basis of schizophrenia?
explanation: EXPLANATION: DISC1 is one of the most important candidate genes for schizophrenia. It is one of the most researched genes in schizophrenia, alongside the COMT AND NRG1 genes. DISC1 is a protein that performs many functions, including neuronal migration, intracellular transport, synaptic maintenance, and stabilisation. NRG1 is one of the most important proteins for the variety of functions in which it is involved. Among them are the growth and development of the epidermis and development of the nervous system (synaptic plasticity).
reference: Nastase MG et al. Genetic polymorphism and neuroanatomical changes in schizophrenia. Romanian Journal of Morphology and Embryology. 2022 Apr;63(2):307.

stem: Which of the following neurotransmitters has been shown to be sensitive to epigenetic tuning in the context of maternal attachment?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Oxytocin is a crucial regulator of human social behaviour. Individual differences within the oxytocin system – assessed through hormonal levels, epigenetic modification, or genetic variation - have been linked to differential sensitivity to social cues, prosocial behaviours, and stress responsiveness in adults. Early experience in maternal care predicts epigenetic change within the infant oxytocin system, levels of which are in turn reflective of infant temperament.
reference: Krol KM et al. Epigenetic dynamics in infancy and the impact of maternal engagement. Science Advances. 2019 Oct 16;5(10):eaay0680.

stem: Motor speed is best assessed by which of the following tests?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Finger tapping is a standard measure of simple motor speed. It is particularly useful for documenting lateralised motor impairment.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 53.

stem: A non-dominant cerebral hemisphere lesion is most likely to lead to which of the following?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Symptoms arising from non-dominant hemisphere injury tend to be subtle, and predominantly neuropsychologic. The cause is usually a structural lesion, such as trauma, stroke, or malignant tumour, that has rapidly developed in the non- dominant parietal or frontal lobe cortex. Neuropsychological deficits include constructional apraxia (Gestalt), dressing apraxia, and anosognosia.
reference: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9th Edition. 2023. pp. 168-169.

stem: Which of the following is part of the default mode network?
explanation: EXPLANATION: The default mode network is an integrated system of cortical areas that are active in a person who is in a state of wakeful rest, daydreaming, reminiscing, or contemplating future events, but not focused on a specific task involving the sensory (especially visual) input. It includes the medial prefrontal cortex, the posterior cingulate gyrus, and angular gyrus, and the medial, lateral, and inferior parietal lobe (IPL), and parts of the parahippocampal gyrus. The attached picture (from Schimmelpfennig J, et al. Frontiers in human neuroscience. 2023 Mar 20;17:1133367) displays the other major neurocognitive networks; note that IPL is not exclusively a DMN-only region.
reference: Menon V. 20 years of the default mode network: A review and synthesis. Neuron. 2023 May 10.

stem: Which of the following is the best test for selective attention?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Stroop tests are based on the fact that it takes longer to call out the colour names of coloured patches than to read words, and even longer to name the colour of an ink in which a colour name is printed when the print ink is a colour different from the colour name. The latter phenomenon, a markedly slowed response when a colour name is printed in ink of a different colour, is interpreted as a failure of selective attention.
reference: Hodges JR. Cognitive assessment for clinicians, 3rd Edition. 2018. p. 248.

stem: According to ICD-11, how many episodes of depression are needed for a diagnosis of recurrent depressive disorder?
explanation: EXPLANATION: In ICD-11, recurrent depressive disorder is characterised by a history of at least two depressive episodes separated by at least several months without significant mood disturbance.
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: In ICD-11, which of the following features is characteristic of children with reactive attachment disorder?
explanation: EXPLANATION: In ICD-11, reactive attachment disorder is characterised by grossly abnormal behaviours in early childhood, occurring in the context of a history of grossly inadequate child care. Even when an adequate primary caregiver is newly available, the child does not turn to the primary caregiver for comfort, support, and nurture, rarely displays security-seeking behaviours towards any adult, and does not respond when comfort is offered.
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: According to ICD-11, which of the following may be seen in OCD but not in hoarding disorder?
options: Accumulation of excessive amounts of objects
Hoarded objects have an intrinsic value
explanation: EXPLANATION: Individuals with OCD may accumulate excessive amounts of objects (i.e. compulsive hoarding). However, unlike hoarding disorder, the behaviour is undertaken with the goal of neutralising or reducing concomitant distress and anxiety arising from obsessional content such as aggressive, sexual/religious, contamination, or symmetry/ordering themes. Furthermore, even in individuals affected by OCD who have poor or absent insight, the behaviour is generally unwanted and distressing, whereas in hoarding disorder it may be associated with pleasure or enjoyment. Generally in hoarding disorder, items are hoarded because of their emotional significance, instrumental characteristics, or intrinsic value (e.g. perceived aesthetic qualities).
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: In ICD-11, what is the minimum duration of grief response required for a diagnosis of prolonged grief disorder to be made?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Prolonged grief disorder is a disturbance in which, following the death of a person close to the bereaved, there is a persistent and pervasive grief response characterised by longing for the deceased or persistent preoccupation with the deceased accompanied by intense emotional pain. In ICD-11, the grief response must have persisted for an atypically long period of time following the loss (more than 6 months at a minimum).
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: Which of the following is a specifier for a depressive episode in ICD-11?
explanation: EXPLANATION: In ICD-11, available specifiers for a depressive episode include: with prominent anxiety symptoms; with panic attacks; persistent; with melancholia; with seasonal pattern.
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: As defined in ICD-11, which of the following best differentiates complex PTSD from PTSD?
options: Avoidance of memories of traumatic events
A series of continued traumatic events
explanation: EXPLANATION: Whereas the ICD-11 diagnostic requirements for complex PTSD include all essential features of PTSD, the diagnosis of complex PTSD also requires the additional essential features of severe problems in affect regulation, persistent negative beliefs about oneself, and persistent difficulties in sustaining relationships.
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: Which of the following is an interviewer-rated scale?
explanation: EXPLANATION: The Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HAM-D) is an interviewer-rated, 17-item rating scale for depressive illness. It is not a diagnostic instrument, but is used to measure changes (e.g. as a result of drug treatment). 17 items are scored according to severity, producing the final score.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 97.

stem: What is an advantage of using a cross-sectional method to study developmental phenomena in children?
options: Avoids the confounding effect of age
explanation: EXPLANATION: One advantage of using a cross-sectional method in studying developmental phenomena in children is that it allows for quick data collection from participants of different age groups at a single point in time. This method is efficient for obtaining a snapshot of developmental trends across different age cohorts, but it does not provide longitudinal insights into individual development or establish temporal causality. Attrition rates can vary, and the use of this design alone does not inherently improve response rates.

stem: Which of the following is a test of pre-morbid intelligence?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Since the ability to pronounce irregular words correctly is highly educationally dependent, a test of irregular word reading, the National Adult Reading Test (NART), is widely used to predict premorbid intellectual disability.
reference: Hodges JR. Cognitive assessment for clinicians, 3rd Edition. 2018. p. 80.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate test for abstract reasoning?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Abstract reasoning is the ability to shift back and forth between general concepts and specific examples. Having the patient identify similarities between like objects or concepts (apple and pear, bus and airplane, or a poem and a painting) as well as interpreting proverbs are useful ways to assess one’s ability to abstract.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 11.

stem: According to ICD-11, which of the following is seen in anorexia nervosa, but not in avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Individuals with anorexia nervosa (AN), like individuals with avoidant- restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID), present with a pattern of restricted eating and significantly low body weight, with similar health-related consequences. The difference is that in AN, behaviours to establish or maintain an abnormally low body weight are usually explicitly motivated by a desire for thinness or an intense fear of gaining weight. In ARFID, the pattern of eating behaviour is not motivated by preoccupation with body weight or shape.
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: A young child appears frozen after hearing a loud noise but does not come close when offered comfort. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: EXPLANATION: In ICD-11, reactive attachment disorder is characterised by grossly abnormal behaviours in early childhood, occurring in the context of a history of grossly inadequate child care. Even when an adequate primary caregiver is newly available, the child does not turn to the primary caregiver for comfort, support, and nurture, rarely displays security-seeking behaviours towards any adult, and does not respond when comfort is offered.
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: When public health campaigns aim to influence behaviour by detailing the harms of smoking and the benefits of not smoking, this is best attributed to which type of power, according to classic work of French & Raven?
explanation: EXPLANATION: According to French & Raven, informational power stems from the logical or persuasive content of the communication between the influencing agent and the target. Informational power is used when campaigns explain the reasons for recommended behaviours, indicating how such behaviours would contribute to improved heath.
reference: Brown JH, Raven BH. Power and Compliance in Doctor/Patients Relationship. REVISTA LEX MERCATORIA Doctrina, Praxis, Jurisprudencia y Legislación. 1994;6(1):3-22.

stem: The unintentional distortion of memory that occurs when it is filtered through a person’s current emotional, experiential, and cognitive state is best referred to as
explanation: EXPLANATION: Retrospective falsification refers to the unintentional distortion of memory that occurs when it is filtered through a person’s current emotional, experiential, and cognitive state. It is often found in those with depressive illness who describe all past experiences in negative terms due to the impact of their current mood. Any psychiatric illness can lead to retrospective falsification, which is related to insight of the patient as well as to suggestibility.
reference: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 66.

stem: What Gestalt principle of perception is shown in this figure?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Proximity is one of the four original grouping laws of Gestalt psychology that explain the organisation of parts into whole by the visual system. According to the law, elements close together tend to be grouped perceptually, so that the array OO OO OO OO tends to be perceived as four pairs rather than eight separate elements.
reference: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015. p. 611.

stem: Hypoplasia of which of the following structures has been associated with autism spectrum disorder?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Cerebellar hypoplasia was an early documented change in brain morphology in ASD (autism spectrum disorder). The finding of cerebellar hypoplasia in ASD has been replicated and has been associated with the loss of cerebellar Purkinje cells in the posterior lobe whose degenerated myelinated axons contribute to reduced cerebellar volume.
reference: Welsh JP et al. Intellectual disability and cerebellar hypoplasia in autism reported by associative learning. medRxiv. 2021 Mar 28:2021-03.

stem: The cocktail party phenomenon involves
explanation: The cocktail party phenomenon involves selective attention in speech perception that enables a listener to attend to one among several equally loud conversations occurring simultaneously, factors such as voice quality and directional cues facilitating the task. Recordings of conversations under similar circumstance are very much harder to understand. The term was introduced in 1957 by the British telecommunications engineer Colin Cherry.Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015. p. 140.

stem: A child goes to daycare for the first time. He shows no reaction when he is left by his parents and no reaction when they come back. What type of attachment does this describe?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Mary Ainsworth devised the Strange Situation procedure with 12- to 18- month infants, which categorised infant-parent relationships. The procedure involves separations and reunions with caregivers and observes response. In insecure (anxious)- avoidant attachment, the child seems unconcerned at separation or reunion. It is associated with unresponsive parenting.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 658-659.

stem: Which of the following is not a strength of the nomothetic personality theory approach (which categorises specific and fixed domains to personality clusters)?
options: Personality seen in terms of attributes
explanation: EXPLANATION: There are two main approaches to conceptualise and describe variations in personality: nomothetic and ideographic. In nomothetic approaches, personality is seen in terms of attributes shared by individuals. There are two subdivisions: type (or categorical) approaches – in which there are discrete categories of personality - and trait (or dimensional) approaches – in which a limited number of qualities, or traits, account for personality variation. Unlike nomothetic approaches, ideographic approaches on the other hand, emphasise individuality and seek to understand an individual’s personality by understanding that specific individual and their development, rather than by reference to common factors. Examples include psychoanalytic, humanistic, and cognitive-behavioural approaches.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 520.

stem: Which of the following is true regarding the classical categorical classification of disorders?
options: Disorders are overlapping and not distinct
Disorders appear in more than once in the system
It facilitates collection of epidemiological data
It allows for varying levels of severity
correctAnswer: It facilitates collection of epidemiological data
explanation: EXPLANATION: In classical categorical systems, each entity or disorder is distinct and appears only once in a clearly defined place. With a few exceptions, ICD and DSM are such classical categorical systems. WHO member states are responsible for reporting health statistics based on ICD to WHO (e.g. causes of morbidity and mortality, prevalence). ICD remains structured as a categorical taxonomic system because this format is necessary for its application as the classification system for global health statistics. Wide use of non-standard categories would not generate valid data for global health statistics.
reference: Clark LA et al. Three approaches to understanding and classifying mental disorder: ICD-11, DSM-5, and the National Institute of Mental Health’s Research Domain Criteria (RDoC). Psychological Science in the Public Interest. 2017 Nov;18(2):72-145.

stem: Which of the following is true of the Kaiser CDC Adverse Childhood Experiences Study?
options: Parental divorce was included as an adverse childhood experience
Psychological abuse was not included in the original study
The study utilised a questionnaire mailed to households in the UK
Exposure to childhood abuse and household dysfunction showed no relationship to
There was a significant relationship between the number of childhood abuse categories and depression as an adult
correctAnswer: There was a significant relationship between the number of childhood abuse categories and depression as an adult
explanation: EXPLANATION: The CDC-Kaiser Permanente adverse childhood experiences (ACE) study is one of the largest studies of the long-term relationship of childhood experiences to important medical and public health problems. The ACE study questionnaire was mailed to over 13 000 adults in California, USA, with a 70% response rate. Seven categories of adverse childhood experiences were studied: psychological, physical, or sexual abuse; violence against mother; and living with household members who were substance abusers, mentally ill or suicidal, or ever imprisoned. Persons who had experienced four or more categories of childhood exposure, compared to those who had experienced none, had 4 to 12-fold increased health risks for alcoholism, drug abuse, depression, and suicide attempts. The study found a strong graded relationship between the breadth of exposure to abuse or household dysfunction during childhood and multiple risk factors for several of the leading causes of death in adults.
reference: Felitti VJ et al. Relationship of childhood abuse and household dysfunction to many of the leading causes of death in adults: The Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) Study. American journal of preventive medicine. 1998 May 1;14(4):245-58.

stem: In altruism research, which of the following is a replicated finding?
options: Altruism can reduce the physical perception of pain
Altruism is an exclusively human behaviour
Performing altruistic behaviours does not improve well-being
correctAnswer: Altruism can reduce the physical perception of pain
explanation: EXPLANATION: Altruistic behaviours occur among many animals, including humans. It is well-documented that performing altruistic behaviours has a positive effect on psychological well-being and health. There is also evidence that performing altruistic behaviours relieves physical pain.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1041.Wang Y et al. Altruistic behaviors relieve physical pain. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 2020 Jan 14;117(2):950-8.

stem: Increased maternal sensitivity during attachment behaviour is due to increased functional connectivity of which structures?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Maternal sensitivity consists of the accurate interpretation followed by prompt and appropriate response to the infant’s signals. It is a well-documented predictor of attachment. The hippocampus and amygdala are key components of the limbic system that are centrally implicated in socio-emotional functioning. The amygdala plays a salient role in orienting to and processing emotionally significant information. The hippocampus is central to learning and memory. The hippocampus and amygdala are activated during interactions between infants and their caregivers.
reference: Bernier A et al. Mother–infant interaction and child brain morphology: A multidimensional approach to maternal sensitivity. Infancy. 2019 Mar;24(2):120-38.

stem: According to Piaget’s theory of development, what is the most important feature of the sensorimotor stage?
explanation: EXPLANATION: According to Piaget, the critical achievement of the sensorimotor stage is the development of object permanence or the schema of the permanent object. This relates to the child’s ability to understand that objects have an existence independent of their involvement. Infants learn to differentiate themselves from the world and maintain a mental image of an object, even when it is not visible.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1007.

stem: If a child wants to t in socially and be described as a ‘nice person’, he is exhibiting which level of Kohlberg’s theory of morality?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Lawrence Kohlberg integrated Jean Piaget’s concepts and described multiple stages of moral development within three significant levels of morality. The first level is pre-conventional morality, in which punishment and obedience are the determining factors. The second level is conventional morality, in which right and wrong are defined in terms of convention and ‘what people would say’. Children try to conform to gain approval and maintain good relationships with others and are also guided by rigid codes of ‘law and order’ (authority orientation). The third and highest level is the morality of self-accepted moral principles (post-conventional), in which children voluntarily comply with rules based on a concept of universal ethical principles and make exceptions to rules in certain circumstances.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 902. Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015. p. 167.

stem: Which of the following is defined as the ‘meaning of words’ in linguistics?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Lexical semantics is the study of word meaning. Phonology, orthography, syntax, and phenomenology are all relevant aspects of linguistics, but they deal with different aspects of language, such as sound patterns (phonology), written symbols (orthography), sentence structure (syntax), and subjective experiences (phenomenology), respectively. Lexical semantics specifically deals with the meaning of words themselves.
reference: Alonso-Sánchez MF, Ford SD, MacKinley M, Silva A, Limongi R, Palaniyappan L. Progressive changes in descriptive discourse in first episode schizophrenia: a longitudinal computational semantics study. Schizophrenia. 2022 Apr 12;8(1):36.

stem: Which of the following antidepressants has the least sexual side effects?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Of the antidepressants, agomelatine, bupropion, and vortioxetine have the best evidence supporting a more favourable sexual side effect profile. Among the tricyclic antidepressants, sexual dysfunction is more common with clomipramine, amitriptyline, and imipramine. Overall evidence suggests relatively high rates of sexual dysfunction across all the SSRIs.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 405-406.

stem: Clozapine has the most affinity to which receptor?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Clozapine binds most potently to alpha 1A/B receptors. Though it has 5HT2A/D2 antagonism, numerous binding properties have been identified for clozapine, most of which are more potent than its binding at the D2 receptor. Clozapine’s blocking of alpha 1 adrenergic receptors can cause dizziness, hypotension, and syncope.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscienti c Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 217. Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. p. 193.

stem: Which of the following drugs is most likely to be abused by students who are studying for exams?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Smart drugs’ (also known as ‘nootropics’) are used by healthy subjects (i.e. exam-taking students and worker) typically to improve memory, attention, learning, executive functions and vigilance. The most popular drugs are amphetamine-type stimulants, methylphenidate, donepezil, selegiline, moda nil, piracetam, benzodiazepine inverse agonists, and uni ram analogues.
reference: Schifano F et al. Benefits and harms of ‘smart drugs’(nootropics) in healthy individuals. Drugs. 2022 Apr;82(6):633-47.

stem: What is atomoxetine’s mechanism of action?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Atomoxetine is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (NRI). Sometimes called NET inhibitors, the selective NRIs have known antidepressant properties. However, despite its name, atomoxetine enhances both dopamine and norepinephrine in the frontal cortex, presumably accounting for its therapeutic actions on attention and concentration in ADHD.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscienti c Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 407. Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. p. 83.

stem: Which type of glutamate receptor is linked to G-proteins?
explanation: EXPLANATION: There are several types of glutamate receptors, including the neuronal presynaptic reuptake pump (EAAT) and the vesicular transporter for glutamate into synaptic vesicles (vGluT). Metabotropic glutamate receptors are those glutamate receptors that are linked to G proteins. NMDA, AMPA, and kainate receptors for glutamate are all members of the ligand-gated ion-channel family of receptors (also known as ionotropic receptors or ion-channel-linked receptors).
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscienti c Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 99-101.

stem: Which of the following antipsychotics reaches peak plasma concentration the earliest?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Peak plasma concentrations of: quetiapine are reached in 1-1.5 hours; olanzapine within six hours; sulpiride in 3-6 hours; aripiprazole within 3-5 hours; iloperidone within 2-4 hours.
reference: Mauri MC et al. Clinical pharmacology of atypical antipsychotics: an update. EXCLI journal. 2014;13:1163.

stem: In pharmacokinetics, what does ‘area under the curve’ denote?
options: Time to reduce plasma concentration by ½
Time to maximum concentration of the drug
Time until the drug is fully eliminated
explanation: EXPLANATION: The ‘area under the curve’ (AUC) is the total drug dose from time 0 to infinity. It represents the total drug dose or drug burden.
reference: Currie GM. Pharmacology, part 2: introduction to pharmacokinetics. Journal of Nuclear Medicine Technology. 2018 Sep 1;46(3):221-30.

stem: Which of the following is true in first order kinetics?
options: A constant fraction of drug is eliminated per unit of time
A constant amount of drug is eliminated per unit of time
A log of plasma concentration plotted against time will show non-linear decay
A graph of plasma concentration plotted against time will show linear decay
The rate of elimination is independent of drug concentration
correctAnswer: A constant fraction of drug is eliminated per unit of time
explanation: First-order kinetics (blue plot) is when a constant (exponential) fraction of drug is eliminated per unit of time. It is similar to the concept of radioactive decay. First-order elimination follows an exponential trend and can be displayed with a logarithmic y-axis to generate a straight line. Zero-order kinetics (red plot) is when there is a constant (linear) rate of drug elimination, indicating that the rate of elimination is independent of drug concentration. Unlike first-order kinetics, a constant amount of drug is eliminated per unit of time. Plot created using jupyter notebook (matplotlib)
reference: Currie GM. Pharmacology, part 2: introduction to pharmacokinetics. Journal of Nuclear Medicine Technology. 2018 Sep 1;46(3):221-30.

stem: Absorption of a drug is generally independent of
explanation: EXPLANATION: Factors that influence drug absorption include the molecular size of the drug, lipid solubility of the drug, degree of ionisation of the drug, dosage form (e.g., tablet or solution), chemical nature of the drug, whether there is complex formation, pharmacological effect of the dose and concentration of the drug, blood ow (at the side of administration), site of absorption, and route of administration.
reference: Currie GM. Pharmacology, part 2: introduction to pharmacokinetics. Journal of Nuclear Medicine Technology. 2018 Sep 1;46(3):221-30.

stem: When patients comply with medications simply because the drugs are recommended by doctors, this is best attributed to which type of power, according to the classic work of French & Raven?
explanation: EXPLANATION: According to French & Raven, expert power stems from the target (patient) attributing superior knowledge and/or ability to the influencing agent (doctor). Explanations or reasons are not necessary for the patient to comply with the doctor’s recommendations.
reference: Brown JH, Raven BH. Power and Compliance in Doctor/Patients Relationship. REVISTA LEX MERCATORIA Doctrina, Praxis, Jurisprudencia y Legislación. 1994;6(1):3-22.

stem: Ebstein anomaly is most associated with which drug?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Lithium use during pregnancy has a well-known association with the cardiac malformation, Ebstein anomaly. Of note, however, is that more recent data suggest that the magnitude of the effect is much smaller than previously estimated.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 690.

stem: Metabolic syndrome was present in what percentage of patients in the CATIE trial?
explanation: EXPLANATION: In the CATIE trial, metabolic syndrome prevalence was 41% and 43%, respectively, using the National Cholesterol Education Program (NCEP) and AHA (fasting glucose threshold of 100mg/dl) derived criteria.
reference: McEvoy JP et al. Prevalence of the metabolic syndrome in patients with schizophrenia: baseline results from the Clinical Antipsychotic Trials of Intervention Effectiveness (CATIE) schizophrenia trial and comparison with national estimates from NHANES III. Schizophrenia research. 2005 Dec 1;80(1):19-32.

stem: Hallucinogenic effects of psychedelics are produced by activity on which receptor?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Hallucinogens such as LSD, psilocybin, and mescaline are 5HT2A agonists. When these agents stimulate 5HT2A receptors on glutamatergic pyramidal neurons in the prefrontal cortex, this causes overactivation of the glutamate neuron. The resultant release of glutamate into the ventral tegmental area causes hyperactivity of the mesolimbic dopamine pathway, resulting in delusions and auditory hallucinations. Excessive glutamate release in the visual cortex can cause visual hallucinations.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscienti c Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 135.

stem: Which of the following drugs has the narrowest therapeutic index?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Some drugs have a narrow therapeutic index (a small increase in dose can cause toxicity and a small reduction in dose can cause a loss of therapeutic action). The most commonly prescribed ones are digoxin, warfarin, theophylline, phenytoin, carbamazepine, and lithium.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 602, 787.

stem: Which of the following is the most biologically important metabolite?
explanation: EXPLANATION: Oxazepam is a short-acting benzodiazepine and one of the most frequently prescribed anxiolytic drugs. It is also the active metabolite of a wide range of other benzodiazepines, such as diazepam, ketazolam, temazepam, and chlordiazepoxide.
reference: Dinis-Oliveira RJ. Metabolic profile of oxazepam and related benzodiazepines: clinical and forensic aspects. Drug metabolism reviews. 2017 Oct 2;49(4):451-63.

stem: Which of the following best describes the primary mechanisms of action of lurasidone?
options: Antagonist at D2; agonist at 5HT2A and 5HT7
Agonist at D2; antagonist at 5HT2A and 5HT7
explanation: EXPLANATION: Lurasidone is a 5HT2A/D2 antagonist. It also potently blocks 5HT7 receptors, which may be beneficial for mood, sleep, cognitive impairment, and negative symptoms in schizophrenia, and also in bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder. Lurasidone lacks potent actions at D1, M1, and H1 receptors, theoretically suggesting less propensity for inducing cognitive impairment, weight gain, or sedation compared to other agents with these properties.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscienti c Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 236. Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. p. 457.

Disorders of Visual Perception Choose the term that best applies to each of following scenarios. 1. When a man with schizophrenia first looks at a friend's face, it appears normal, but the face then transforms to be frighteningly grotesque and misshapen.

2. Despite not having any pets, an elderly woman with visual impairment intermittently sees cats in her apartment, which delight her.

3. Upon seeing a shadow, a recently bereaved man briefly thinks that it is his deceased wife.

CORRECT ANSWERS: 1) When a man with schizophrenia first looks at a face, it appears normal, but the face then transforms to be frighteningly grotesque and misshapen. - Paraprosopia 2) Despite not having any pets, an elderly woman with visual impairment intermittently sees small cats in her apartment, which delight her. – Hallucination 3) Upon seeing a shadow, a recently bereaved man briefly thinks that it is his deceased wife. - Illusion EXPLANATION: Metamorphopsia or dysmegalopsia refers to change in the perceived shape of an object. When metamorphopsia affects faces, it is referred to as paraprosopia. Faces generally transform into a grotesque mask (monster, vampire, werewolf). Autoparaprosopia is a term used to describe a phenomenon where an individual perceives a transformation or alteration in their own facial appearance while gazing into a mirror. Note that paraprosopia is a distortion of reality seen in conditions such as schizophrenia and is seen as a delusional misidentification similar to Capgras and Fregoli delusions), while the term prosopagnosia is an inability to identify faces seen in organic conditions affecting brain's face recognition area. Charles Bonnet syndrome is a condition in which complex visual hallucinations occur in the absence of any psychopathology and in clear consciousness. It is associated with either central or peripheral reduction in vision and not surprisingly is most common in the elderly, although it can occur in younger people also. These visual hallucinations can be accompanied by pleasure and amusement.

stem:
Tests of neuropsychological functioning Choose the test that best assesses the following neuropsychological functions.

1. Motor speed

2. Abstract reasoning

3. Working memory

4. Visuospatial construction

5. Set shifting

CORRECT ANSWERS: 1) Motor speed – Finger Tapping 2) Abstract reasoning – Interpreting Proverbs 3) Working memory – Digit Span 4) Visuospatial construction – Clock Drawing 5) Set shifting – Wisconsin Card Sorting EXPLANATION: Finger tapping is a standard measure of simple motor speed. It is particularly useful for documenting lateralised motor impairment. Abstract reasoning is the ability to shift back and forth between general concepts and specific examples. Having the patient identify similarities between like objects or concepts (apple and pear, bus and airplane, or a poem and a painting) as well as interpreting proverbs are useful ways to assess one's ability to abstract. Working memory is synonymous with short-term memory, which is responsible for the immediate recall of small amounts of verbal (as in digit span) or visuospatial information. Clock drawing is a useful technique for assessing constructional ability and is also sensitive to organisation and planning. The best formal test of set shifting is the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, which also involves problem-solving and hypothesis testing. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 11, 53.

stem:
Neurons and Glial Cells Identify the cell responsible for each of the following functions.

1. Phagocytosis of cellular debris

2. Nutrition of neurons and release of glutamate

3. GABA-ergic projection in the striatum

4. Myelination in the central nervous system

5. Myelination in the peripheral nervous system

CORRECT ANSWERS: 1) Phagocytosis of cellular debris - Microglia 2) Nutrition of neurons and release of glutamate - Astrocytes 3) GABA-ergic projection in the striatum – Medium spiny neurons 4) Myelination in the central nervous system – Oligodendrocytes 5) Myelination in the peripheral nervous system – Schwann cells EXPLANATION: There are three types of glial cells. The most common are the astrocytes, which have several functions, including nutrition of neurons, deactivation of some neurotransmitters, and integration with the blood-brain barrier. The astrocyte carries most of the extracellular glutamate. The oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system and the Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system wrap their processed around neuronal axons, resulting in myelin sheaths that facilitate the conduction of electrical signals. The third type of glial cells, the microglia, which are derived from macrophages, are involved in removing cellular debris following neuronal death. The functions of microglia in the non-diseased brain probably include a role in synaptic maintenance. GABA-ergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs), the principal neuron type in the striatum, are projection neurons with predominantly dopaminergic and glutamatergic inputs. The loss of MSNs in the striatum is the hallmark of Huntington disease. Ref: Siracusa R et al. Astrocytes: role and functions in brain pathologies. Frontiers in pharmacology. 2019 Sep 27;10:1114. Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 924.

stem:
Specialised Cells Identify the cell responsible for each of the following functions. (Answers may be used more than once.) 1. Cells responsible for rapid signal transmission between brain regions

2. Principal neuron type in the cerebral cortex responsible for cortical processing

3. Specialized neurons associated with social cognition and self-awareness.

4. Inhibitory interneurons that regulate neural activity in cortical circuits

5. Star-shaped glial cells involved in synaptic integration in the brain.

CORRECT ANSWERS: 1. Cells responsible for rapid signal transmission between distant brain regions - Pyramidal cells 2. Principal neuron type in the cerebral cortex responsible for cortical processing - Pyramidal cells 3. Specialized neurons associated with social cognition and self-awareness - Von Economo neurons 4. Inhibitory interneurons that regulate neural activity in cortical circuits - Basket cells 5. Star-shaped glial cells involved in synaptic integration in the brain - Astrocytes

EXPLANATION: A diverse set of specialised cell types collectively contribute to the complex functions of the brain. Pyramidal cells serve as the principal excitatory neurons responsible for rapid signal transmission between brain regions and cortical processing in the cerebral cortex. von Economo in 1925 did pioneering work on the cytoarchitectonics of the cerebral cortex and discovered a specialized and unique cell

(VENs) appear as large sticks, rods or corkscrew cells because of their extremely elongated and relatively thin cell body which is distinct from the more common oval or spindle-shaped infragranular neurons. Basket cells, specialised cells first described by Ramon y Cajal, are inhibitory interneurons in the neocortex, cerebellum and hippocampus; they form 'baskets' of axonal arborizations onto and around the somata of target neurons. Astrocytes, characterized by their star-shaped morphology, play a multifunctional role in the brain, including synaptic integration, regulation of neurotransmitters, nutrient support for neurons and overall brain homeostasis. Ref: Siracusa R et al. Astrocytes: role and functions in brain pathologies. Frontiers in pharmacology. 2019 Sep 27;10:1114. Boland R, Verduin M. stem:
Adverse effects of psychotropic medication Identify the drug most likely to have caused the following side effects.

1. Weight loss

2. Worsening psoriasis

3. Rash

CORRECT ANSWERS: 1) Weight loss - Topiramate 2) Worsening psoriasis – Lithium 3) Rash - Lamotrigine EXPLANATION: Topiramate can cause nausea, appetite loss, and weight loss. Topiramate is an antiepileptic medication that is also used as an adjunct treatment for mood disorders and binge-eating disorder. One of its notable side effects is appetite suppression, which often leads to weight loss in individuals taking the medication. Patients may also experience nausea, which can contribute to decreased food intake and, consequently, weight loss. Some skin conditions such as psoriasis and acne can be aggravated by lithium. 10-14% of patients receiving lamotrigine will develop rash. Most are benign. A minority may be serious/life-threatening skin reactions requiring hospitalisation (e.g., Steven- Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, angio-oedema, and a rash associated with several systemic manifestations). Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber's Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. pp. 781-782. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 358. Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 250.
